desc:
An AI use policy for staff sets clear, safe sharing rules in words your team will read. Ecom Swift LLC writes a short policy covering approved tools, data that must stay private, checks before content reaches customers, and what to do after a mistake.

## What is an AI use policy?

An AI use policy is a short internal document that tells staff how they may use AI tools at work. It names the tools your business approves, lists the information that must never be pasted into them, says who checks the output and explains what to do if something goes wrong.

It is a practical rulebook, not a legal contract. Our work is a plain-language policy for your team and does not replace advice from a lawyer where you need it.

## Why you need rules before someone makes a mistake

Public chat tools are easy to use, and that is the risk. A well-meaning employee pastes a customer list into a chat window to tidy it, or a contract to get a summary, or a draft reply that includes a private order detail. Nobody meant to cause harm, yet the information has left your control.

The other risk is quality. An unchecked answer sent to a customer can contain a wrong promise or an invented fact. Without a rule that says who reviews output before it goes out, each person decides alone, and standards drift.

## How a clear policy improves your business

A policy removes guesswork. When people know exactly what is allowed, they use the tools with more confidence and fewer second thoughts, which means more of the benefit and less of the worry. Owners also gain a reference point for onboarding new staff and for answering customers who ask how you handle their information.

The mechanism is simple. Short rules with examples are remembered; long documents are not. A one page summary on a shared wall or chat channel keeps the rules in front of people at the moment they are about to paste something. Results still depend on whether staff follow the rules, so we include roles and sign-off to support that.

## What a good AI use policy contains

- A list of approved tools, and a note on how new tools get approved.
- Data that must never be shared, such as customer lists, passwords, payment details and private contracts.
- Plain examples of acceptable and unacceptable use.
- Rules for customer data handling.
- A named person who checks output before it is sent to customers.
- Guidance on content that customers will see, such as emails, posts and product text.
- A description of how to use the tools honestly with clients and colleagues.
- Steps to take if information is shared by mistake.
- A sign-off sheet where staff confirm they have read the rules.
- A one page summary for quick reference.

## What we write for you

We begin by learning which tools your team already uses, what kind of information your business handles and who deals with customers. Then we write the policy to fit. The Basic package gives you a one page policy with an approved tools list, a never-share list and examples. Standard delivers a fuller policy, roles for checking output, customer data rules, a staff sign-off sheet and a one page summary. Premium builds a pack with a short handbook, incident steps, rules for customer facing content, a quiz and a briefing for managers.

Add-ons include customer notice wording, a staff quiz and a review call to go through the policy together.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Use short sentences and real examples from your own business.
- Name an owner for the policy, so questions have a place to go.
- Tell staff which tools are approved and why.
- Explain what to do after a mistake, without blame.
- Review the policy when you adopt a new tool.

**Avoid:**
- Banning every tool, which pushes people to use them in secret.
- Writing rules so long that nobody finishes them.
- Allowing staff to paste customer details into free tools.
- Leaving output unchecked when it goes to customers.
- Keeping the policy in a folder nobody opens.

## Who this is for

This service suits a small agency whose staff already use chat tools and whose owner worries about client files. It suits a shop with a support team answering customers all day. It also suits a business preparing for a client review that asks how it handles data and AI.

## What we need from you

Tell us which AI tools your team uses, the kinds of information you hold, and any rules you already have. Send examples of the work staff do with the tools. We never need passwords or account access, because the policy is built from conversation and documents. If you have a privacy notice or client contract that mentions data handling, send it so our wording stays consistent with it.
